core_condition: at least one measured effect recorded in observed_effects from Ventora telemetry or public corpora

evidence.rationale: The most experimentally developed body in S7. Mayer's programme has produced controlled studies of each principle over three decades, synthesised in the Cambridge Handbook and 'Nine Ways to Reduce Cognitive Load'. The corpus carries 49 meta-analyses and systematic reviews, including Richter, Scheiter & Eitel on signalling, Ginns on spatial and temporal contiguity, Höffler & Leutner and Berney & Bétrancourt on animation versus static images, and Mayer, Heiser & Lonn (2001) establishing the coherence effect. Principles are specific and separately tested rather than a general claim that visuals are better — which is what makes them operational.

product_applicability.rationale: Directly implementable and cross-cutting: image-carried explanation, coherence pruning, signalling, contiguity and redundancy avoidance apply to landing, onboarding, pricing and dashboard surfaces alike. Reference at scale: side-by-side documentation layouts, demonstration-led product pages, single-focus lesson screens.

measurability.rationale: Reachable proxies: task completion, time to complete, error rate, attention to primary action, conversion. The literature's own outcome — comprehension on transfer tests — is not directly available to us, which is precisely the transfer the dossier flags below.

orthogonality.rationale: Substantially downstream of CL-14 (the principles are applied load management) and adjacent to PS-13 (memory advantage of images) and PF-16 (subjective ease). Retained as a distinct L1 because its content is a set of specific, separately validated combination rules — coherence, signalling, contiguity, redundancy — that neither the capacity constraint nor the memory finding provides. Score 2 for real within-node overlap.

safety.rationale: Applying these principles serves comprehension, which is user-aligned. Three misuse vectors are blocked as hard rules: replacing required information (price, terms, limitations) with imagery; illustrative visuals that overstate what the product does; and visual-first presentation that strips text alternatives and semantic structure, which would trade one group's comprehension for another group's access. Accessibility is treated as a hard constraint rather than a preference.

dissent: The strongest caution is not against the principles but against over-reading them. (1) Domain transfer: virtually the entire evidence base measures learning outcomes — comprehension and transfer tests in instructional settings — not commercial interface outcomes such as conversion, retention or willingness to pay. It is reasonable to expect comprehension gains to help those outcomes, but it is an inference, and it is the specific reason this mechanism enters incubating rather than core. (2) Richer is not better: the animation-versus-static meta-analyses report mixed and modest advantages, and Makransky et al. (2017) found that adding immersive VR to a science simulation produced more presence but *less* learning — a direct warning that engagement and comprehension can move in opposite directions. Any reading of this mechanism as 'add more media' is contradicted by its own literature. (3) Expertise reversal recurs here as in CL-14: signalling and scaffolding that help newcomers can become extraneous for experienced users. (4) The redundancy principle has documented boundary conditions — under some pacing and prior-knowledge configurations, duplicated presentation does not harm and may assist — so it is claimed as a default, not a law. Finally, a note on our own use: the popular reading of this literature as 'people prefer pictures to text' is not what it says. It says relevant images combined with concise words under specific rules outperform prose alone; precise, sequential and technical information is often better carried by text, and stripping necessary language would be a misapplication of this evidence.
